findings.rationale: NE's uploaded updates are near zero in size: median norm ratio 0.008 against a federation median around 1, with a size-adjusted z of -9.3. Its per-round norm ratios are exactly 0 in about half the rounds (e.g. rounds 5, 8, 9, 12, 13, 15-17, 19, 20) and tiny otherwise, with near-zero or random cosine to the median update. This is the signature of uploading the global model back without training. Small norms are already present in round 1 (0.013), so I date the onset to round 1.

WI's update norms are negligible: median norm ratio 0.004 (size-adjusted z -6.7), with min norm ratio 0.004 and min cos -0.62. Its norm ratio is exactly 0 in several rounds (5, 9, 10, 12, 13, 20), and the rest are small and erratic. Round 1 is already tiny (0.0025), so the fault looks present from the start. Consistent with free-riding rather than poisoning, since the updates are near zero rather than scaled or sign-flipped.

IN's update norms are near zero: median norm ratio 0.0068 (size-adjusted z -7.7), and the norm ratio is exactly 0 in about half the rounds (3, 6, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18). The remaining rounds are much smaller than the federation median, with erratic cosines. This matches uploading the global model without local training. Its norms are already tiny in round 1 (0.022), so I date the onset to round 1.

report.summary: Screened all 52 clients with the all-client views of client_updates, client_performance, drift_by_round, feature_summary and subgroup_outcomes (Sex, AgeGroup, Income), then confirmed with narrower queries. The clearest signal is three clients (IN, NE, WI) whose uploaded updates are near zero in norm (median norm ratio about 0.004-0.008 against a federation median near 1, size-adjusted z between -6.7 and -9.3), with exact-zero updates in many rounds. That pattern fits free-riding, so I report them as free_rider from round 1. Their local performance rows were not flagged, which is consistent with free-riding rather than label noise. Other weak leads did not hold up: the AgeGroup and Sex subgroup outliers (CT, AK, MI, ME, GU, VI, NH) and feature tail outliers (DE, GU, TN, NC, VI, WY, ID, NC) were either within noise at the small per-client epsilon or not confirmed by a second tool. Drift, label-noise and prevalence screens were clean after noise adjustment. Budget was fully spent (20.0 epsilon).
